abstract: This study investigates how political efficacy shapes individuals' selection of political information within algorithmically curated news feeds. Combining survey data with digital trace data from 186 Dutch users' Google Discover usage histories, it examines both within-person changes over time and between-person differences in information-selection behavior. The analysis focuses on three dimensions of political information engagement: the proportion of political content selected, exposure diversity, and (implied) related selection patterns.
key_claims: Political efficacy helps explain individual differences in how people select political information from algorithmic feeds.
Information-selection behavior on algorithmic feeds varies both within individuals over time and between individuals.
Between-person differences in political information selection are conditioned by users' political efficacy.
methods: Combined survey data with digital trace data (usage histories) from 186 Dutch individuals.
Used Google Discover, a fully algorithmically curated feed, as the platform of study.
Analyzed within-person changes in information-selection behavior over time.
Analyzed between-person differences conditioned by political efficacy.
Examined multiple aspects of information selection, including the proportion of political information selected and exposure diversity.
findings: The abstract is truncated and does not report specific results; the study aimed to characterize within-person temporal change and between-person efficacy-conditioned differences in political information selection.
Findings pertain to the proportion of political information selected and exposure diversity (further details not available in the abstract).
contributions: Introduces political efficacy as an explanatory factor for information-selection behavior in algorithmic feeds.
Integrates self-report survey measures with behavioral trace data from a real algorithmic feed (Google Discover).
Distinguishes within-person over-time dynamics from between-person differences in studying algorithmic news exposure.
framing: The paper positions itself within research on algorithmic news curation and selective exposure, using political efficacy from political communication scholarship to explain individual-level differences in engagement with political information on algorithmically curated feeds.
